item.title: ESMA publishes latest edition of its newsletter
item.description:
ESMA publishes latest edition of its newsletter 29 October 2026
ESMA newsletter

The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), the EU’s financial markets regulator and supervisor, has published today the latest edition of its Spotlight on Markets newsletter, covering key activities and publications from September and October 2026.

This edition opens with the appointment of Carlo Comporti as ESMA’s next Chair. His appointment was confirmed by the Council of the European Union, and he will take up his position on 1 November 2026.

Top news highlights include ESMA’s 2027 Annual Work Programme, setting out priorities for stronger, simpler and more integrated EU capital markets; the new Union Strategic Supervisory Priority on digital innovation; and the European Supervisory Authorities’ priorities for 2027.

Other key publications featured in this edition include:

  • the preparations for the transition to T+1 settlement,
  • the ESAs’ call for vigilance over external dependencies, cyber threats and private markets, 
  • ESMA’s proposals to make MiCA clearer, safer and ready for emerging services,
  • and its second Trends, Risks and Vulnerabilities Report of 2026.

Other updates include a Memorandum of Understanding with the Securities and Exchange Board of India, ESMA’s analysis of the continued growth in cross-border investment services, as well as the latest supervisory, regulatory and enforcement developments.

The Spotlight on Markets newsletter is published regularly and is available on ESMA’s website. For regular updates, follow ESMA on LinkedIn, X and Instagram.

item.title: ESMA proposes simpler EU Taxonomy reporting
item.description:
ESMA proposes simpler EU Taxonomy reporting 29 October 2026
Issuer disclosure
Sustainable finance

The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), the EU’s financial markets regulator and supervisor, has published its Final Report providing technical advice to the European Commission on simplifying key performance indicators under the Taxonomy Disclosures Delegated Act.

ESMA recommends narrowing the mandatory operating expenditure (OpEx) KPI to non-capitalised research and development expenditure. It also proposes simpler group Taxonomy reporting, including removing the weighted-average KPI, and targeted measures to make disclosures more proportionate, clearer and easier to use. 

The Technical Advice was coordinated with the other European Supervisory Authorities, in particular on the voluntary use of counterparties’ OpEx information and group-level Taxonomy reporting. 

The proposals support ESMA’s simplification and burden reduction objectives, while focussing reporting on information that is useful for decision-making, and preserving the relevance, comparability and reliability of Taxonomy disclosures. 

Next steps

ESMA has submitted the Final Report and its technical advice to the European Commission for consideration in its review of the Taxonomy Disclosures Delegated Act.

item.title: ESMA streamlines several Q&As as part of simplification efforts
item.description:
ESMA streamlines several Q&As as part of simplification efforts 22 October 2026
Market Abuse
MiFID - Secondary Markets
Short Selling
Simplification and Burden Reduction

The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), the EU regulator and supervisor, has updated its Questions and Answers (Q&As) on market structure under MiFID II, the Market Abuse Regulation (MAR) and the Short Selling Regulation (SSR), removing outdated, duplicative and no longer relevant guidance as part of its Simplification and Burden Reduction (SBR) initiative. 

The exercise focused on identifying Q&As that are no longer relevant due to legislative amendments that are reflected in established market practices, or that are covered by other ESMA guidance. As a result, several Q&As have been withdrawn or amended, including instances where the same issues are addressed in other ESMA publications such as supervisory briefings and opinions. 

The goal of the initiative is to reduce unnecessary complexity, remove obsolete guidance and ensure that ESMA's Q&As remain relevant, proportionate and consistent with the current legislative framework.

Stakeholders are encouraged to refer to the updated set of Q&As together with any other ESMA guidance for the most comprehensive interpretation of the applicable rules.

item.title: ESMA specifies requirements to facilitate safe use of post-trade risk reduction services
item.description:
ESMA specifies requirements to facilitate safe use of post-trade risk reduction services 20 October 2026
Guidelines and Technical standards
Post Trading

The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), the EU’s financial markets regulator and supervisor, has outlined the conditions that providers and users of post-trade risk reduction (PTRR) services need to meet for certain OTC derivative transactions to be exempt from the clearing obligation under EMIR 3. The new rules, published in its latest final report, also establish safeguards for the provision of these services and the monitoring of the use of the exemption.

With these new rules in place, the goal is to facilitate the use of PTRR services and ensure that the exemption is used under the conditions laid down in EMIR 3 and does not lead to the misuse of the clearing obligation.

The final report specifies the elements and requirements of PTRR services, including the information to be provided to participants, how exercises are carried out, the controls that providers should have in place, record-keeping and how the exemption will be monitored.

PTRR services help market participants manage their derivatives portfolios and reduce risks, thereby contributing to safer and more resilient derivatives markets.

The final rules build on existing market practices and aim to avoid introducing additional requirements where existing rules already meet the relevant objectives, in line with ESMA’s simplification and burden reduction objectives.

Next steps

The draft Regulatory Technical Standards will now be submitted to the European Commission for endorsement, in line with the standard review process.

item.title: ESMA finalises the review of guidelines on the delay in disclosure of inside information
item.description:
ESMA finalises the review of guidelines on the delay in disclosure of inside information 16 October 2026
Guidelines and Technical standards
Market Abuse
Market Integrity
Simplification and Burden Reduction

The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), the EU’s financial markets regulator and supervisor, has updated and streamlined its Market Abuse Regulation (MAR) guidelines on the delay in the disclosure of inside information, completing the revised regulatory framework.

Under MAR, issuers are required to disclose as soon as possible the inside information concerning them, to ensure that investors are informed and to prevent insider dealing. In specific circumstances, issuers may delay public disclosure to avoid prejudicing their legitimate interests. 

These guidelines help issuers in their decision to delay disclosure by providing a non-exhaustive list of legitimate interests that could justify such delay. Following a public consultation, ESMA has identified five additional legitimate interests for delaying disclosures, covering the following situations:

  • where the issuer is requested not to disclose information by a public authority;
  • where the issuer needs to collect additional information to enable a correct assessment of inside information by market participants;
  • where the issuer may risk the loss of a business opportunity following the disclosure of sensitive commercial information;
  • where the appointment of a member of the issuer’s governing body or a manager holding a key position could be jeopardised;
  • where the disclosure of inside information concerning companies within the same group could cause a direct prejudice to the issuer and undermine the effectiveness of the delay applied by other company.

Since June 2026, issuers are no longer required to immediately disclose inside information related to protracted processes before their completion. As a result, and in line with its simplification and burden reduction objectives, ESMA has removed from the current guidelines the legitimate interests for delayed disclosure connected to these processes.

Next steps

The revised guidelines will become applicable from the date of their publication on ESMA’s website in the 24 official languages of the European Union.

item.title: One year to go for T+1 settlement: the regulatory framework is complete, now let’s make it happen
item.description:
One year to go for T+1 settlement: the regulatory framework is complete, now let’s make it happen 16 October 2026
Guidelines and Technical standards
Post Trading
Press Releases

The European Union (EU) will switch to T+1 settlement on 11 October 2027. Ahead of the transition, the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), the EU’s financial markets regulator and supervisor, calls on market participants to finalise technical preparations, assess readiness across their entire ecosystems and begin testing as soon as possible throughout the trading and settlement chain.

With the publication of the RTS and ESMA Guidelines on standardised procedures and messaging protocols, the regulatory framework is now ready. The first deadline is for investment firms and their clients to comply with the new requirements on allocations and confirmations from 7 December 2026.

Verena Ross, ESMA’s chair, said: 

“The transition to T+1 is one of the most impactful recent market structure initiatives. It will fundamentally improve the efficiency and international competitiveness of the EU markets.  The date is known, the roadmap is clear, and, with the final piece of regulatory guidance published today, the framework is now in place for all players in the trading and settlement chain to prepare for 11 October 2027. 
A successful transition is a shared effort by the industry and the public authorities. The focus now shifts to market participants to comply with the regulatory requirements, ready their systems and processes, and test their preparedness for the change, considering the recommendations of the EU T+1 Industry Committee.” 

Delivering the final piece of regulatory work

ESMA’s revised guidelines on standardised procedures and messaging protocols clarify how market participants should meet the new requirements on allocations and confirmations introduced by the amended RTS on Settlement Discipline, in particular, as of 7 December 2026, the mandatory use of: 

  • electronic, standardised communication channels and international messaging standards; and 
  • machine-readable communication methods, except in cases of temporary technical disruptions.

item.title: ESMA updates its manual on transparency with new guidance for OTC derivatives and tick-size regime
item.description:
ESMA updates its manual on transparency with new guidance for OTC derivatives and tick-size regime 15 October 2026
Trading

The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), the EU regulator and supervisor, has updated its manual on transparency to provide further guidance on the identification of over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives subject to transparency requirements and to enhance supervisory convergence on the application of the tick-size regime.

The update also clarifies how the identifying reference data for OTC derivatives should be provided for transparency purposes, supporting greater consistency in the data reported to and published through the consolidated tape. 

The manual finally includes several published Q&As on the tick size regime, as well as the addition of recommendations on the application of the tick-size regime, comprising when trading venues and national competent authorities may intervene in specific circumstances.

Next steps

With regard to the guidance on OTC identifying reference data, the updated manual should be considered a draft until the entry into force of the related technical standards (RTS 2 and RTS on CTP input/output data).

item.title: ESMA's third Sanctions Report highlights the need for greater convergence in enforcement
item.description:
ESMA's third Sanctions Report highlights the need for greater convergence in enforcement 15 October 2026
Market Abuse
Supervisory convergence
Transparency

The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), the EU's financial markets regulator and supervisor, published today its consolidated report on sanctions and measures imposed across the European Economic Area (EEA) in 2025, enhancing the transparency of sanctions data reported under EU financial acts within its remit.

In 2025, national authorities across the EEA imposed more than 950 administrative sanctions and measures, a stable number compared with the past two years. The aggregated value of administrative fines amounted to almost €82 million. The report also highlights an increased use of settlements.

As in previous years, activity remained focused mainly on breaches of the Market Abuse Regulation and the Markets in Financial Instruments Directive and Regulation. Enforcement activity remained concentrated in a small number of jurisdictions, with Germany, France and Spain accounting for two thirds of the total value of administrative fines across the EEA. 

Need for stronger convergence

The report highlights significant differences in enforcement, including in the number and type of sanctions imposed, the level of fines and the use of settlement procedures. The findings point to a need for stronger convergence in enforcement, particularly where limited enforcement activity cannot be explained by market size.

Supervisory effectiveness ultimately depends on market participants’ compliance with the rules, and should not be measured solely by the number or value of the sanctions imposed in a Member State. Nevertheless, enforcement actions are an important component of the supervisory toolkit.

Next steps

Building on the findings of this report, ESMA will further continue to foster exchanges among national securities and markets authorities on the effective and consistent implementation of capital markets rules, including through case discussions. The objective is to ensure that similar breaches result in similar enforcement outcomes across the EU, irrespective of where they have been committed. 

The underlying data are available in excel format. In addition, a snapshot of the report’s key findings is published here.

item.title: ESMA analysis shows continued growth in cross-border investment services
item.description:
ESMA analysis shows continued growth in cross-border investment services 14 October 2026
Investor protection

The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), the EU’s financial markets regulator and supervisor, has completed its annual analysis of the cross-border provision of investment services, together with national competent authorities (NCAs).

The exercise collected data from investment firms across 30 jurisdictions in the EU/EEA and found that cross-border investment activity continued to grow significantly in 2025.

Key findings:
  • A total of 379 financial firms provided cross-border services to retail clients.
  • Approximately 15.5 million clients in the EU/EEA received investment services from firms located in other Member States, almost twice as many as in 2023.  
  • Compared to 2024:
    • The number of firms increased by 2%.
    • The number of retail clients rose by 47%.
    • Complaints remained stable (decreased by -0.2%).
  • Cyprus remained the primary location for firms providing cross-border investment services in the EU/EEA, accounting for 20% of passporting firms, followed by Luxembourg (14%) and Germany (12%).
  • France, Spain, Germany and Italy are the main destinations for retail clients receiving cross-border services in other Member States.

These findings will support ESMA and the NCAs in monitoring cross-border investment services and understanding developments affecting retail investors across the EU/EEA.

Next steps

ESMA will carry out the next data collection in 2027.
